output.myth: Kael the Netter cast his net off the north cliffs for a star that had come down too low. The net came up heavy, but it held a gull instead. It was a grey gull with a wet wing and a cry like a broken latch, and it was not the star, and Kael swore at it the way he swore at everything. But the gull looked up at him with the look of a bird that knows the wind, and his hands were slow that morning. He thought of his own mother, who had gone aloft as a kite the winter the Gale took the boats. So he unhooked the gull and opened his hands. Tavo laughed, as Tavo does, and took the gull up. Kael never caught another star that year, and he did not mind much. The gull still flies between the lamps with the mark of the net on one wing. When you see it turning over the north cliffs, that is the Netter's good mistake, and Hesk, who keeps count of everything, counts it kindly.
output.verse:
Kael's net came up full
the gull, not the star, he freed—
net-marked, it wheels still.
